questions.q: What is the main argument of the article?
options: Saying no preserves time and beats optimizing your work
Successful people should say yes to every opportunity
Meetings are the main cause of low productivity today
Politeness matters more than managing your own time
questions.explain: The article argues that not doing something is always faster, and elimination beats optimization.

questions.q: Which programming saying does the author compare to saying no?
options: Premature optimization is the root of all evil
There is no code faster than no code
Write once, run anywhere is the goal of design
Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code
questions.explain: The author cites the saying that there is no code faster than no code.

questions.q: How does the author describe saying yes versus saying no?
options: Yes is a time credit and no is a time debt
Both carry roughly equal weight
Yes is time debt and no is time credit
Yes is a luxury and no is a duty
questions.explain: No is a form of time credit; yes is a form of time debt you must pay back.

questions.q: What does McKeown suggest saying to a manager who asks you to take on a new project?
options: Say you will do it once your current work ends
Say you are too busy and suggest a coworker instead
Say yes now and renegotiate the deadline later
Ask which other projects to deprioritize for it
questions.explain: The note advises asking which other projects to deprioritize to make the new one the priority.

questions.q: What does the author imply about how your approach should change as you succeed?
options: Raise your bar and decline even previously good opportunities
Start saying yes to more things as your skills improve
Stop worrying about distractions once you have succeeded
Delegate all of your meetings to others on your team
questions.explain: He says opportunity cost rises with success, so you must upgrade your no's and decline formerly good uses of time.
